checkpoints: A token bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills continuously at refillPerSec.
Refill is lazy — there is no background timer running for any bucket.
Refill is instead computed the moment a request arrives, from elapsed time since a stored timestamp: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsedSeconds * refillPerSec).
Each allowed request removes exactly the tokens it needed.
A client that has been quiet accrues tokens up to capacity purely from that elapsed-time formula, then can spend them all at once in a burst before settling back to the average refill rate.

A fixed-window counter resets hard at every window boundary, so a client can send a full window's traffic at the end of one window and another full window's worth at the start of the next — nearly double the intended rate.
The token bucket avoids that boundary-straddling doubling while still letting a normal user's legitimate bursts through.
A fixed-window counter buckets requests by clock minute (e.g. a key like rl:user:202606051203) and resets the counter to zero every time the minute rolls over.

A client can fire the full 100 requests at second 59 of the current minute — hitting the limit — and then, right at second 0 of the next minute, the counter has already been reset to zero, so it grants another 100 requests.
The result is 200 requests slipping through in 2 seconds — double the rate the system thought it was enforcing.

The bug isn't in the counting itself (the counter adds correctly within each minute) — it's the hard reset at the boundary: the counter has no memory whatsoever of requests that happened just an instant before.

Making the window "slide" means dropping the whole idea of a "clock-minute bucket" and replacing it with a trailing window: at any given moment, the request count is however many requests happened in exactly the last N seconds counted backward from right now, moving continuously with every incoming request instead of standing still and jumping each time the minute changes.
With a genuine trailing window, the situation above can't happen: the 100 requests at second 59 are still inside the window at second 60 of the next minute, so request 101 gets rejected.

There are two ways to actually implement this sliding — an exact way, recording every single timestamp and evicting whatever has fallen out of the window; and an approximate way, estimating the count in the trailing window by weighting the previous window's contribution based on how much time has elapsed into the current one.

Each reject branch in a compensating cascade must DECR exactly the set of tiers that were already INCRed above it in that same run — here the tenant-reject branch never DECRs the user key it INCRed, and the global-reject branch DECRs only the tenant key while leaving the user key permanently inflated.

Because bump() increments the user tier before the tenant and global verdicts are known, a reject at either later tier leaves the earlier tiers' counters holding an increment that was never actually granted unless it is explicitly rolled back before returning.

The fix is mechanical: add redis.call('DECR', KEYS[1]) on the tenant-reject branch, and add the same DECR on the user key alongside the existing tenant DECR on the global-reject branch, so every reject path fully undoes everything incremented before it.

This increment-then-conditionally-reject pattern behaves like a small saga — each rollback must undo every prior step's effect, not just the immediately preceding one, whenever a later step in the cascade fails.

The leak produces no error and no crash because every individual redis.call the script issues (GET, INCR, PEXPIRE, the one DECR it does call) succeeds on its own terms; the bug is a missing call rather than a failing one, so there is no exception path or log line to surface it.

The visible symptom is gradual over-throttling rather than an outage: userCount and, on a global reject, tenantCount silently drift upward relative to the number of requests actually granted, so identical traffic gets throttled more tightly over time with no error to point to.

Keeping the whole increment-check-rollback sequence inside one EVALSHA/Lua script call keeps the compensation atomic, so no other request evaluated through the same cluster.evalsha call can ever observe the user or tenant counters in their briefly over-incremented state.

Correctness of the fix is proven by driving traffic that rejects at each tier in turn — user, tenant, global — and asserting afterward that userCount, tenantCount, and globalCount each equal exactly the number of requests actually granted at or below that tier, with zero residual drift.

Sending the full Lua script body via EVAL on every consume call re-transmits roughly a kilobyte of text per request, and Redis must hash (and recompile, if it isn't already the cached script) that body before running it — a cost that scales linearly with RPS instead of staying flat.

This is a transport/bandwidth problem, not a correctness problem: the Lua script already executes atomically on Redis's single thread, and that guarantee is unaffected by how the script text reaches the server.
Calling SCRIPT LOAD once — for example in onModuleInit — registers the script body with Redis and returns a 40-character SHA1 digest that can be cached on the service instance for reuse.

Replacing eval(LUA_TOKEN_BUCKET, ...) with evalsha(sha, ...) sends only the short digest per request instead of the full script body, cutting per-call payload from roughly a kilobyte down to about 40 bytes.

The refill-then-deduct logic inside the Lua script itself does not change at all — only the wire format of how the client invokes it changes, so the algorithm and its atomicity are identical before and after the optimization.

Switching to EVALSHA introduces a new failure mode: if Redis restarts or a SCRIPT FLUSH runs, the server no longer has the script cached, and calling evalsha with the old SHA throws a NOSCRIPT error even though the client still holds a valid-looking digest.

A NOSCRIPT error needs to be caught and handled by reloading the script (SCRIPT LOAD again, or a one-off EVAL fallback for that single request) and retrying with the freshly reloaded SHA, so a single cache flush never takes the rate limiter down.

The improvement should be confirmed with a before/after load test: correctness stays intact (a concurrency=20 run against capacity=5 still yields allowedActual: 5), while p99 latency and CPU per request should visibly drop once only the digest travels per call instead of the full script text.

A sliding-window log limiter that stores one ZSET member per in-window request keeps memory usage proportional to request volume, so a client sustaining ~10k requests per minute ends up with ~10k entries live in Redis for that key alone.

Each admission check on that log pays `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` (evict expired entries) plus `ZCARD` (count survivors), an O(log N + M) cost — and because N grows with traffic, the busiest keys are exactly the ones paying the highest per-check cost, which is the wrong direction for a hot path.
A weighted two-bucket counter replaces the per-request log with just two integers per client, `curr` and `prev`, one for the current window-sized bucket and one for the previous.

The sliding count is estimated as `prev * (1 - elapsedRatio) + curr`, fading the previous bucket's contribution smoothly as the current bucket fills rather than resetting sharply at a window boundary; this turns both memory and per-operation work into O(1), independent of request volume.

This estimator is an approximation, not an exact count — it trades a small, known error (on the order of 0.003% at reasonable traffic) for eliminating the O(N) memory blow-up and the eviction/count cost on hot keys.

Because the counter is approximate, any use case where the count itself is the source of truth — billing, contractual/hard quotas, audit trails — needs to stay on the exact ZSET log; only clients that are both genuinely hot and tolerant of a small margin of error should be migrated to the counter.

Rolling out a new counting mechanism as a drop-in replacement for an exact one carries a correctness risk that can't be resolved by inspection alone — it needs to be validated against the structure it's replacing under realistic load before being trusted for real traffic.

That validation takes the form of running both implementations side by side — driving the same requests through the exact log and the new counter and comparing their outputs — and confirming the counter's estimate stays within the accepted error bound at the target request rate before any hot client is actually cut over to it.
Key layout is three keys per tenant sharing one hash-tag: user `{q:<tenantId>}:u:<userId>`, tenant `{q:<tenantId>}:t`, and global `{q:<tenantId>}:g`.

The shared tag is not decoration — Redis Cluster picks a key's slot by hashing only the substring inside the first `{...}`, so the same tag forces all three keys onto one slot/one node, the precondition for running a multi-key script atomically at all.
Contract is `check(tenantId, userId) -> { allowed, blockedAt: "USER" | "TENANT" | "GLOBAL" | null, userCount, tenantCount, globalCount }`.
Per-tier limits and the window length are passed in as inputs, and each key's TTL is bounded by that window length.
The cascade order lives inside the atomic operation itself: cheapest tier (user) first, then tenant, then global, so the innermost ceiling rejects before any shared resource is touched.

The compensation rollback also lives inside the atomic operation: decrement exactly the tiers already bumped when a later tier rejects, so a request blocked at tenant does not silently leak a unit of user quota.

`blockedAt` beats a bare boolean because a caller that only gets `false` can't log, alert, or tell the tenant anything useful, while `"TENANT"` names precisely which ceiling to back off from and powers per-tier observability.

The hash-tag lives inside the key itself rather than as a separate call parameter because slot routing is a property of the key's own bytes — passing the tenant id as a separate argument next to an untagged key would not pin anything, and the three tiers could land on three different slots, causing any multi-key script over them to be rejected outright.
Gives the exact contract signature: `consume(key, capacity, refillPerSec, tokens = 1)` returning `{ allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs }`.

States refill and deduct happen inside ONE atomic step executed entirely by the store (e.g. a single Lua script run start-to-finish on Redis's single thread) — never as two separate caller-side calls.

Names the concrete failure mode of splitting refill/deduct into two calls: concurrent callers all read the same stale token count and each independently decides there's room, over-granting past capacity.
States retryAfterMs is derived from the deficit and refillPerSec (e.g. `ceil(deficit / refillPerSec * 1000)`), not just returned alongside a bare `allowed: false`.
States remaining exists for observability (dashboards/logs) and plays no role in the allow/deny decision itself.

Argues the clock source matters: caller-supplied `now` is fine for a single node but breaks once many pods have skewed clocks, so the store should read its own clock (e.g. Redis `TIME`) inside the atomic step.
States the store owns all durable bucket state (token count, timestamp, TTL) while the caller owns only the intent (how many tokens, right now).
States the contract is host-agnostic — identical whether called from NestJS, Spring, ASP.NET, or Go — because the atomic script itself is the same regardless of caller language.
The 6th call is denied because the bucket has fully drained (`tokens=0`), so `remaining` stays at 0 rather than going negative.
The deficit is computed as `deficit = requested - tokens = 1 - 0 = 1`.
`retryAfterMs = ceil((deficit / refillPerSec) * 1000) = ceil((1 / 1) * 1000) = 1000` milliseconds, exactly matching the number in the response.

The client should wait exactly that long before calling again — typically surfaced via a `Retry-After` header — instead of retrying immediately or applying an arbitrary backoff unrelated to the bucket's actual state.

Returning a concrete `retryAfterMs` is better than a bare 429 because it turns rate limiting into a cooperative protocol where both sides agree exactly when it's worth trying again, cutting down amplified retry load compared to a client guessing or applying a generic backoff.
Across 5 users at 5 requests each, 25 requests clear the USER tier, so a per-user cap alone would not be enough to contain this tenant.
The TENANT tier (cap 20) is the actual binding constraint.
Exactly 20 requests clear all three tiers, and the other 30 are rejected with `blockedAt = "TENANT"`.
Those 30 rejected requests never reach the GLOBAL tier, and compensation DECRs back every inner INCR, so the shared 50-ceiling stays mostly free.

Other tenants still keep their fair share of the global quota because the tenant layer holds the abuser back before it can starve the shared resource — something a single global counter could never do.
States GET-check-SET is three separate round-trips (GET, decide, SET) with a gap between the read and the write, not one atomic operation.

Names the concrete race: with capacity=5 and 20 concurrent requests across pods, all 20 GET the same stale 'tokens remaining' snapshot before any SET lands, so each independently concludes there's room (a lost update).
States the over-grant scales with concurrency/pod count — so a limit of 5 can let all 20 requests through instead of exactly 5.

States no client-side fix (smarter retries, added delays, etc.) can patch this, because the flaw is that read and write are separate commands on shared server state that no client can observe another client touching in between.
States the real fix must make the read-and-write indivisible on the server holding the state, not on the calling client.
Explains Lua fixes this because Redis is single-threaded and executes an entire Lua script as one command, run to completion, before serving any other client's command.
States wrapping the read (e.g. HGET/HMGET), refill, deduct, and write (HSET) inside that one script removes the gap — no other request can interleave between the read and the write.
States that with the atomic fix in place, capacity=5 and 20 concurrent requests yields exactly 5 winners, not more.
